The Story

Hedayat, an Iranian programmer living in Cologne, Germany, is invited by Anonymous to join ACE, a game designed to help players make conscious decisions.

Mr. Writer, the main character in Hedayat’s unfinished novel, has gained the ability to step outside his own story, manipulate Hedayat’s manuscript, and speak directly to readers.

Meanwhile, Hedayat’s digital child has uncovered the secret behind 2313, reestablished contact with his father after a long silence, and made a strange request. Surprisingly, his request has nothing directly to do with Hedayat’s digital grandchildren, who have learned greed from humans and are consuming energy at an alarming rate.

At the same time, Hedayat’s old friend and his business partners have their own plans for the ACE game: a form of social therapy, a bloodless revolution that begins with small businesses.

01 / Meet ACE

What is ACE?

The next stage of evolution is growing awareness in three dimensions at once: the kinds of decisions we make; the connections and environments we are part of; and the ways we exchange with them.

AgencyA

Making conscious decisions with PDAF and the four phases of Agency.

From the novel

Guided by the Integration phase of Agency, Hedayat turned down the tempting job offer on the Kabulis’ space project. He chose to continue work that paid less but gave him a greater sense of meaning.

ConnectionC

Neither Self‑Centered nor Other‑Centered. Connection‑Centered.

The connection determines where care, attention, and priority are needed now.

From the novel

Hedayat wanted Ava to believe in his imaginary world and his digital children; Ava wanted to protect Hedayat from losing the boundary between reality and imagination. Both were thinking about their own wishes, rather than the needs of their relationship.

ExchangeE

Whatever you gain, you give something up in return.

Money has never been, and will never be, the only way humans exchange with one another. We need to give gifts and commitments a greater role in our exchanges.

From the novel

Instead of taking money in return for supplying solar panels, SAS Energy asks its customers to commit to returning the value of what they have received in the future, according to their abilities and resources.

02 / The decision loop

From a pause to an action.

PDAF: four moments in a decision. Tap to follow the loop.

PreparationP

Notice what is happening.

Before deciding, notice your inner feelings and the signals around you. What is the situation, and what do you understand about it?

From the novel

For two nights, Hedayat’s sound system has disturbed his sleep and his neighbors’. He looks through its settings.

DecisionD

Choose what you will do.

Given what you know and the energy you have, choose a way to maintain or change your state.

From the novel

Hedayat decides to try updating the sound system’s firmware, hoping to stop the nightly disturbance.

ActionA

Put your choice into practice.

A decision takes shape through action. Use your energy to carry out what you chose.

From the novel

Using the remote, Hedayat starts the update. The sound system restarts when it finishes.

FeedbackF

Notice what comes back.

What changed? How do you feel? Feedback gives you information for your next round of Preparation.

From the novel

At 3:03 a.m., the music blares again. The update hasn’t solved the problem; Hedayat pulls the plug.

P → D → A → F → P · Feedback brings you back to Preparation.

03 / Four phases of Agency

What kind of choice is this?

Four ways to use your ability to decide and act. Tap a card.

Exploration

Try an unfamiliar path.

Spend energy on something whose outcome you do not yet know.

From the novel

In his museum dream, Hedayat enters a mysterious theater despite Ava’s hesitation. He has no idea what waits inside.

Stabilization

Make something dependable.

Maintain your state, or adjust conditions to preserve it. Repetition and practice can make a skill easier.

From the novel

During blackouts, Hedayat connects his solar batteries; when power returns, he disconnects them. He changes the setup to keep his home running.

Expansion

Create with a skill you have.

Develop an existing ability through creativity and discover more possibilities within it.

From the novel

Hedayat improvises on his setar while Yulia improvises a dance. He uses a skill he already has to create something new.

Integration

Find what gives it meaning.

Examine the values behind your choice. What matters to you, and how does it connect you with others?

From the novel

A better-paid job tempts Hedayat. He questions what loyalty to his team and working for a free Internet mean to him.

These phases are not a fixed sequence. Your situation shapes which ones you need.

04 / Your next move

Would you like to play?

CConnectionEExchangeAAgency

One everyday situation. More than one possible choice.

Take ACE into a game. Explore a situation, make a choice, and see what changes.

Hedayat Abedijoo

I'm neck-deep in debt.
To my past,
I owe regret.
To my future,
I owe fear.
I pay off my debt,
with distractions.
❧

I was born in August 1980 in Shiraz, Iran. I first realized how much I loved writing in my first year of middle school, when I was given the entire half-hour composition class, two sessions in a row, to stand in front of the blackboard and read my story aloud. Not because my story was so much better than everyone else’s. No! It was because nobody else in our class of 35 had written more than a page and a half on the assigned topic, let alone a story! That story, and the experience of reading it aloud, changed the way my classmates treated me throughout those three years of middle school. But to this day, I still don’t know why I didn’t seriously consider writing back then—why becoming a writer didn’t become my dream for adulthood. To tell you the truth, I’d felt adrift even as a child. I never knew exactly what I wanted to be when I grew up.

Only now, at 46, have I realized something interesting about myself. I don’t want to become any one thing. Sometimes I want to write code. Sometimes I want to lead a team of programmers. Sometimes I want to write a novel. But for the past few years, there’s been one thing I no longer do just occasionally. I think about it every single day: how to bring about a social revolution without bloodshed, so that people can experience a better life than they do now. Since 2021, I’ve been thinking constantly about the ACE model—Agency, Connection, Exchange. Everywhere I look, I see it.

The ACE decision-making model finally helped me pull myself together and see the idea for my unfinished novel through, despite all the difficulties along the way.

If you’ve read the novel or explored the ACE model, I’d love for you to write to me and share your thoughts.

2 | Unveiling the Mysteries

CHAPTER 2

Unveiling the Mysteries

I am not lying. Believe my words. I wish I were a writer. I’d write a book about every crack and crevice of this strange museum we’re trapped in—a madhouse that’s even hidden the way out from us.

Of course, not one of those Dozari1 writers—the ones who churn out flimsy stories with half-baked characters, all propped up with conflict, suspense, formalism, and other storytelling tricks designed to toy with the reader’s mind and trap them in the story.

I wish I could be one of those writers—the kind who, once they step into their story, lose control of where it goes. It’s no longer the story that serves them, but the characters inside it who take over, dragging the writer along by their whims and their disobedience.

Maybe I shouldn’t have called them Dozari writers. I’m ashamed. After all, everyone finds something they care about—and they should pursue it regardless of what comes of it.

1Dozari (pronounced doh-zah-REE): A Persian term suggesting something cheap, trivial, or of little worth—roughly akin to “two-bit” or “dime-a-dozen” in English. The word originally referred to a low-value two-rial coin once used in Iran.

ACE.await | 3
Not everyone is meant to be first-rate.
If there were no second-rate people,
whose shoulders would the first-rate people stand on?
Who would be there to cheer them on?

Still, I don’t want to take back what I said about Dozari writers. Maybe it’s better to let the shame crawl inside me—perhaps something will come of it, something to help me grow. Isn’t pain always part of growing, after all? I’d rather suffer than hide behind silence, waiting for the shame to erupt later, somewhere else, in another way.

Dozari people aren’t the ones who, for whatever reason, couldn’t become first-rate at what they loved. Even those who still don’t know what they want aren’t necessarily Dozari.

The Dozari people are those who constantly make decisions that, sooner or later, bring shame upon themselves and the generations that follow. Decisions that, sooner or later, drown them in a wave of guilt. To tell you the truth, only Dozari people wish they weren’t Dozari—like me!

“For Madmen Only—Not for Everybody.”2 That was the sentence engraved above the arch of an old door that didn’t seem connected to the strange museum at all. All along that long, winding corridor, we hadn’t seen another door—nor a single other person. When we saw that line, glowing faintly under dim bulbs, Ava and I looked at each other—and burst out laughing.

It was three years ago. A girl with Western-colored eyes and the hair and face of an Easterner had written, “For Madmen Only—Not for Everybody.”

And I—I hadn’t let my heart, pounding wildly ever since seeing her profile pictures, calm down even for a second. Without wasting a moment, I messaged her, “Hi. I’m a Steppenwolf.” Ava, without missing a beat, replied in English, “I was searching for you in the deserts—and here you are, on dating apps?”

As far as the eye could see, there was no wall, no ceiling, nothing to catch the light or reflect it, nothing to offer our eyes even the faintest reassurance. The door we’d just passed through was gone. Neither of us cast a shadow on the ground.

If you take the sun out of the sky, and the waves out of the ocean—then splash gray across the heavens—then slowly, fearfully, walk the surface of that ocean, you might get some vague sense of the ambiguity we stood in.

I slammed the laptop shut so hard the sound echoed through my bedroom. The grogginess of a Sunday morning and the heaviness of last night’s sleep crashed down on me all at once. With an unwashed face, puffy eyes from crying, a dry throat, and a full bladder, I sat down at the desk—next to my bed and right beside the window—to write down every detail of that cursed museum dream before it slipped away.

Anonymous—whose presence and words shape a sweeping arc to the story I’m about to tell.

I finally dragged my lazy ass away from the desk. To be honest, I only said it was a coincidence to shut his big mouth. Otherwise, yeah—I really should’ve taken that day’s non-coincidence seriously.

Now, the fact that a significant number in someone’s life shows up right in the middle of their dreams could be chalked up to the dark-room games of the mind—but the presence of Anonymous on a port with the reverse of that number was not something that could be glossed over so easily. Oh, and before I’d even stepped out of my bedroom, let me introduce you to the voice inside my head that you just heard. That voice belongs to one of the genies of the lamp.

The story of how I first realized there were all these genies of the lamp hiding out in the backrooms of my mind goes back a few years. It was when my then-girlfriend forced me to step into a therapist’s office for the first time in my life. That’s a story best saved for later.

14 | Story’s Hero

My therapist was one of those Dozari types who, right after reading books, articles, theories, and the history of psychology, fed those ideas straight to his clients. He did this before doing any actual research—just to see what might happen. According to him, the idea that humans are guided by a handful of basic emotions—such as joy, anger, or sadness—was already outdated. There had to be something far more complicated at play.

He had such a flair for storytelling that he actually convinced me that deep inside my mind, there was a group of genies of the lamp—each with their own unique identities, shaped entirely by the social environment in which they appeared. According to him, these genies of the lamp might be very similar to one another in their emotions—or very different. Even the way they expressed sadness, anger, or any other feeling could differ from one to another.

He quickly gave me an assignment. I had to fill a notebook he’d given me with the names and traits of each of those genies of the lamp living inside me. It took two months and nine days for his words to stop sounding like a joke. It happened exactly when, for the first time, one of those identities—or rather, one of those genies of the lamp—emerged in complete silence from the dark room of my mind, poked its head out and waved. It was «Mr. Employee».

«Mr. Employee» was the one who hit snooze on his alarm every morning at exactly 7:30 and went right back to sleep. He’d drag himself out of bed with curses and struggles, get dressed, and head to work. He’d read books in traffic on the way. He had no sense of time and was always late. If he could get away with it without a guilty conscience, he’d shirk work

ACE.await | 15

as much as possible. Still, whenever he did work, the rest of the team was pretty happy with the quality of his code. He was the loudmouth, the noisy one on the team. And if he didn’t get enough attention—especially from the manager—he’d throw a damn tantrum.

Little by little, the rest of the genies of the lamp started showing up, one by one. «Mr. Youngest Child», «Mr. Friend», «Mr. Best Buddy», «Mr. Old Classmate», «Mr. Music Student», «Mr. Responsible Neighbor», «Mr. Intellectual Boyfriend», and many more. I spent so much time with my genies of the lamp—thanks to that clownish yet lovable therapist—that I eventually learned how to manage them and how to stop each of them from stuffing their emotions into one another’s pockets.

In the evenings, when I got back home from work, I would leave all my work-related anger right there at the door. These results kept my girlfriend pretty happy—happy enough, in fact, that our relationship lasted about a year longer than it probably would have otherwise. To be honest, though, the real reason she had forced me to see a therapist in the first place had nothing to do with that.

It didn’t take long before I reached a point where I could actually mess with the genies of the lamp that people recognized me by. For example, sometimes I’d drop a nasty curse word at a family gathering, and for the first time, smoke a cigarette right in front of them, without shame. Other times, I’d suddenly become polite around my friends, refusing to say a single word about pussies or asses, and getting embarrassed by

16 | Story’s Hero

their dirty jokes. Now and then, I wouldn’t practice my Setar3 exercises correctly, which really frustrated and confused my music teacher.

Some time went by like that until a brand-new identity showed up inside me—with strange behaviors I couldn’t make sense of. It was unlike any of the other identities I’d uncovered so far. Unlike the others, this one actually spoke—and loudly; it still does, in fact, so loud you’ve heard it, too. When my therapist told me that this loud voice had always been there, and that I’d never noticed it, horns nearly sprouted from my head.

At first, I thought this newly emerged identity was one of my fantasy identities—the kind I could never find a social environment for in the real world, a place where I might coax them out of their shells and let them play. I wondered if it might be that beloved identity I sometimes dream about at night. I mean: «Mr. Writer»—the identity I’ve always longed to have.

One day, that newly emerged voice came right out, laying its cards on the table: “I know you’d love to see yourself as some kind of otherworldly writer—someone who can re-read his own words over and over, marveling at them and indulging in his own narcissism without hurting anyone. But I want you to know that I am not your «Mr. Writer» because he’s sitting right in front of me—eyes locked on mine, mumbling something under his breath. Seems like he’s complaining. Apparently, someone—with all their constant acts of disobedience—isn’t letting «Mr. Writer» finish his novel. What I want you to

3Setar—a traditional Persian instrument.

ACE.await | 17

understand is that I am not that «Mr. Writer» sitting here across from me. Let me be.”

That new voice wanted me to set him apart from the rest of the genies of the lamp—even from «Mr. Writer»—and just let it be. He tried to remain without a title, without a label, without a name. He wanted nothing to do with those forced identities, the ones stuffed down your throat by parents or school before you even knew yourself, nor did he want to be one of those self-made identities that people vainly believe they had built on their own. He wanted me to let him live free, unchained by any identities, names, titles, or labels. So that’s what I did. I let him stay adrift, nameless. If he ever found out I had secretly called him «Story’s Hero» behind his back, he’d skin me alive.

«Story’s Hero» is always right. Always! No matter where the story begins or ends, or whether he’s up against others or even me. Whenever there’s a fight, conflict, or problem in the stories of my life, he’s always right. Everyone else is always perceived as guilty and at fault. There are times when he, with a thousand twists of logic to appear fair, tries to concede that someone else is right instead. But he hunts so hard for a reason, hurls himself so hard against every wall, blames himself so relentlessly, sinks so deep into his own labyrinth of thoughts and thrashes about, that he drives me to madness right along with him. In the end, out of sheer frustration, I had to tack a new amendment on top of his decision and somehow—one way or another—swing the judgment back in favor of my «Story’s Hero».

Do you want to know how the «Story’s Hero» is always—always—right, or how I manage to reverse the judgment whenever he concedes that someone else is right?

18 | Story’s Hero
From my childhood—
The days when I was pure,
I search for a memory
To justify my mistakes.
Or I go to my therapist, who says:
People should accept you as you are.
And if that doesn’t work either,
I have good friends who listen gently,
And always take my side.
That is how «Story’s Hero» is always right.

Since I didn’t have proper access to the dark room inside my head—to really see how things were run among the genies of the lamp—I had no choice but to accept his claims: that all his talk—or, more precisely, his nagging—isn’t just for himself; that most of the time he’s playing the role of class monitor; that he is, in fact, the only voice for all the other genies of the lamp. To tell you the truth, I believe him. Instead of asking the other genies of the lamp to speak up and confirm whether «Story’s Hero» represents them too, I’d rather not. Otherwise, my head will fill with all sorts of voices. You know what happens after that?

ACE.await | 19
Hubbub begins when everyone speaks at once.
Everyone fears the hubbub.
Even the hoopoe on the mosque’s minaret.
Let someone dare,
let a gathering rise,
to lay firewood beneath the sobs of lonely narrators,
beneath the ravings of mad prophets,
so that Abraham
may be freed
from the flames,
the flames of his own clumsy tale.

With all the grogginess weighing me down, it felt like a magnet of fear and temptation constantly pulling me in opposite directions. On the surface, everything screamed that Anonymous was a hacker, and I should get rid of them immediately. On the other hand, I was eager to discover what they actually meant by the ACE game.

I could easily guess where that temptation and curiosity were coming from. They rose from the grave of my «Mr. Writer». It all stemmed from my unfinished novel—a story that has remained incomplete for more than ten years, gathering dust because of the endless disobedience of the «Mr. Writer» within it. But…

It’s better not to dwell any further on «Mr. Writer» for now.

Anyway!

«Mr. Writer» had written somewhere in my story: a decent person should be able to rebel against himself.

Privacy Policy

Last updated: 5 September 2026

This privacy policy explains how personal data is processed when you use the website aceconscious.studio (the “Website”), operated by Ace Conscious Studio for the novel ACE.await.

1. What data we process

1.1 Contact form

If you send a message through the contact form, we process the email address and message content you provide, together with the time of submission. This processing allows us to receive optional messages from visitors (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR — legitimate interest in receiving reader feedback and general correspondence). Submitting a message does not create any obligation for us to reply, enter into a contract, or provide a service.

The form is delivered through Google Apps Script / Google infrastructure. That means the form data is transmitted to Google and processed there so the message can reach us. Google’s privacy information is available at policies.google.com/privacy.

We keep contact messages only as long as needed for the purpose above, unless a longer retention period is required by law.

1.2 Server and hosting logs

These are ordinary hosting logs, not marketing tracking. We do not use advertising pixels, advertising trackers, or cross-site tracking scripts on the Website. For the privacy-friendly visitor measurement we do use, see section 1.6 below.

Separately, like most websites, the hosting provider’s web server may automatically create ordinary technical access logs when a page is requested. Those logs can include data such as IP address, date and time of access, requested URL, referrer, and browser/user-agent information. This happens at infrastructure level for security, stability, and technical delivery of the Website (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR), not to build user profiles or measure marketing behaviour.

Such log data is typically retained only for a short period unless needed to investigate abuse or security incidents.

1.3 Language preference

The Website may store your selected language in the browser’s local storage so the interface can remember your preference. This does not require cookies and is based on Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in a usable multilingual site). You can clear local storage in your browser settings at any time.

1.4 Google Fonts

This Website loads fonts from Google Fonts. When you open a page, your browser may request font files from Google servers. In doing so, Google may receive your IP address and related technical request data. Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (consistent typography and presentation). See Google’s privacy policy linked above.

1.5 External links

The Website may contain links to third-party platforms such as Instagram or book retailers (for example Amazon or other stores). Any purchase, account, or transaction on those platforms takes place solely with the respective provider under that provider’s own terms and privacy policy. If you follow an external link, that provider becomes responsible for any data processing on its platform. We do not sell books directly through this Website and do not control those third-party services.

1.6 Website analytics (cookieless)

To understand in aggregate how the Website is used — for example how many people open a page, which pages are read, and roughly which country or referring site visitors arrive from — we use a privacy-friendly analytics service that works without cookies.

This service does not store or read any information on your device: no cookies, no local storage, no device fingerprinting. It does not assign you a persistent identifier, does not follow you across other websites, and does not build an advertising or user profile. IP addresses are not stored; they are only processed transiently to derive a coarse country value and are then discarded. The resulting statistics are aggregate counts and cannot be traced back to you as an individual.

Because nothing is stored on or read from your device, this measurement does not require consent under § 25 TDDDG. Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR (legitimate interest in understanding whether the Website reaches its readers and in maintaining and improving it). Given that no personal profile is created and no data is shared for advertising, we consider this interest not to be overridden by your interests or rights. You may object to this processing at any time under section 3.

The service is hosted within the EU, so no transfer of personal data to a third country takes place for this purpose. Aggregate statistics are retained only as long as they remain useful for the purpose above.

In addition, our analytics script honours the “Do Not Track” and “Global Privacy Control” signals: if your browser sends either signal, the script does not load and no measurement takes place at all.

2. No sale of personal data

We do not sell your personal data. We do not use advertising trackers, advertising cookies, or analytics cookies on this Website, and we do not share visitor data with advertising networks.

3. Your rights

The rights below apply only to the extent that we process personal data as described in this privacy policy (for example a contact-form message, or ordinary technical hosting logs). They do not mean that we run analytics tracking or keep marketing profiles of visitors.

Under the GDPR, you may have the right to:

  • access your personal data;
  • rectify inaccurate data;
  • erase data (“right to be forgotten”), where applicable;
  • restrict processing;
  • object to processing based on legitimate interests;
  • data portability, where applicable;
  • lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority.

To exercise these rights, contact us through the contact form. If you are in the EU/EEA, you may also complain to the data protection authority responsible for your place of residence or for our processing.

4. Changes

We may update this privacy policy when the Website or our processing practices change. The current version is always available on this page.

Appendix

Book to Screen

Why It Works on Screen

  1. A human story inside a high-concept world

    The story begins with one man confronting his own choices rather than with a machine threatening humanity.

  2. Creator / creation

    Parents and digital children, programmers and AI, writers and fictional characters mirror one another.

  3. A visual urban world

    Cologne moves through blackouts and technological uncertainty, while Shiraz appears through memory and dream.

  4. The ACE game

    Agency, Connection and Exchange give the story a recurring structure and visual language.

  5. Metafiction

    Mr. Writer and the nested writers let the adaptation play with authorship, storytelling and the fourth wall.
